:::{#exm-exp-memoryless}
#### Remaining survival after 10 event-free weeks

Let $T$ be exponential with rate $\lambda = 0.1$ events per week.
For a subject who has been event-free for $s = 10$ weeks,
the probability of lasting at least $t = 5$ more weeks is:

$$
\ba
\P(T > 15 \mid T > 10)
&= \frac{\ef{-0.1 \cdot 15}}{\ef{-0.1 \cdot 10}}
&& \text{(ratio of survival functions)} \\
&= \frac{\ef{-1.5}}{\ef{-1}}
&& \text{(multiply)} \\
&= \ef{-0.5}
&& \text{(quotient rule for exponentials)} \\
&\approx 0.6065
&& \text{(evaluate)}
\ea
$$

This value equals $\P(T > 5) = \ef{-0.1 \cdot 5} = \ef{-0.5}$,
the probability that a new subject lasts 5 weeks:
the 10 weeks already survived do not change the outlook.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-weibull-not-memoryless}
#### A Weibull distribution with shape 2 is not memoryless (counterexample)

Now let $T$ be Weibull with $\lambda = 0.1$ and $p = 2$,
so $\surv(t) = \ef{-(0.1 t)^2}$ and the hazard increases over time.
Then:

$$
\ba
\P(T > 15 \mid T > 10)
&= \frac{\ef{-(0.1 \cdot 15)^2}}{\ef{-(0.1 \cdot 10)^2}}
&& \text{(ratio of survival functions)} \\
&= \frac{\ef{-(1.5)^2}}{\ef{-(1)^2}}
&& \text{(multiply)} \\
&= \frac{\ef{-2.25}}{\ef{-1}}
&& \text{(square)} \\
&= \ef{-1.25}
&& \text{(quotient rule for exponentials)} \\
&\approx 0.2865
&& \text{(evaluate)}
\ea
$$

whereas $\P(T > 5) = \ef{-(0.5)^2} = \ef{-0.25} \approx 0.7788$.
A subject who has already lasted 10 weeks is less likely to last 5 more weeks
than a new subject is,
because the hazard has risen in the meantime.

:::
